text:
In Genesis 22 no settlement is made between the God who promises and the God who demands; both are kept before the mind, and no sentence is pronounced for either. The reader is left, like Abraham on the mountain, while the knife is raised and the ram has not yet been seen. The question so presented is unanswerable; its being unanswerable is the answer furnished by the chapter. Thus the act of reading becomes a trial, for the chapter gives no release from the perplexity in which it has placed the reader.

At last, therefore, Genesis 22 is more a history of reading than of sacrifice. From it we learn that the matters of greatest weight may lie in what is not said. Abraham is silent; Isaac asks his question; Sarah is absent; the narrator neither explains nor comments. These several omissions and refusals are so many gaps in the narration, and each gap exacts something from the reader. The bareness of the manner is the reader's burden; what is withheld is precisely what is given.
